The Liability of Greenhouse Gas Emitters for Harm Due to Solar Geoengineering Mac Willners a,b,c aDepartment of Philosophy, Stockholm University, Stockholm, Sweden; bInstitute for Futures Studies, Stockholm, Sweden; cStockholm Center on Global Governance, Stockholm University, Stockholm, Sweden

## Abstract

Those who have asked who should compensate for harm due to solar geoengineering have been preoccupied with a version of the Polluter Pays Principle according to which compensatory obliga tions befall deployers of the technology. But there is an alternative (but not mutually exclusive) interpretation. According to it, non deploying greenhouse gas emitters are liable to compensate for harm due to solar geoengineering since they have contributed to the circumstances rendering it an understandable response to the threat of climate change. Such an Emitter Pays Principle is norma tively attractive, especially in cases where deployment is a venial act of self-defense.

ARTICLE HISTORY Received 5 August 2024 Accepted 3 February 2026 KEYWORDS Compensation; solar geoengineering; Polluter Pays Principle; self-defense

## 1. Introduction

Solar geoengineering aims to lower global mean temperatures by decreasing the influx of solar energy. Suggested methods include injecting sulfur aerosols into the stratosphere, brightening marine clouds, and more (Crutzen, 2006; Latham et al., 2012; Shepherd et al., 2009). In light of persistent political inertia in reducing greenhouse gas emissions, interest in such technologies has risen significantly over the past decades (Möller, 2023). Many arguments suggest that the likelihood of solar geoengineering deployment is rising, some stating that it is ‘not a question of if but when’ (Wagner, 2021, p. 15; original emphasis; see also Bostrom et al., 2016; Weitzman, 2015). This provides strong reasons to consider ethical issues in a post-deployment world. One such issue is compensation. Even if solar geoengineering brings net benefits, some will likely be harmed. The best-understood risks include altered precipitation patterns, a heated stratosphere, and ozone depletion (Huynh & McNeill, 2024; Ricke et al., 2023). But often the ‘unknown-unknowns’ of solar geoengineering are considered most worrisome (Keith, 2013, p. 72). Who, if anyone, is liable to provide compensation when harm occurs? Answering this question is crucial for the fairness of solar geoengi neering deployment (Horton et al., 2015; Svoboda & Irvine, 2014, 2015). challenge of answering this question features in an influential argument for a moratorium on developing and deploying solar geoengineering (Biermann et al., 2022). I focus on one particular aspect of the above question. Namely, applying the Polluter Pays Principle to the context of solar geoengineering. The existing, narrow literature has taken for granted that the relevant polluters are the geoengineers. Without a proper argument, it has rejected the alternative (but not mutually exclusive) position that green house gas pollution contributes to solar geoengineering harm. I argue in favor of this position. Sometimes, greenhouse gas emitters are liable to compensate for harm due to solar geoengineering. Section 2 defines the scope of the paper and highlights background assumptions. Section 3 provides an overview of the Polluter Pays Principle and the interpretation of it that will be defended in Section 4. Section 5 elaborates by discussing deployment scenarios. Section 6 responds to objections, and Section 7 concludes.

## 2. Preliminaries

The literature on climate compensation revolves around the Polluter Pays Principle, the Beneficiary Pays Principle, and the Ability to Pay Principle (Caney, 2021). Arguably, combining these is necessary for a just solar geoengineering compensation scheme (Wong et al., 2014). But I am here only concerned with the interpretation of the Polluter Pays Principle according to which greenhouse gas emitters are liable for harm due to solar geoengineering. Thus, whilst any of the principles can, in some scenarios, apportion compensatory obligations for harm due to solar geoengineering onto non-deploying greenhouse gas emitters, I am only concerned with emitters’ liability by virtue of their emissions. The ensuing discussion also presupposes legitimate claims to receive compensation for harm due to solar geoengineering. I assume that such claims can exist, that they are not merely claims to receive aid, and that they are based on modal comparisons. Hence, if one is made temporally worse off by solar geoengineering but would have been even worse off in its absence, one would not be due compensation (but perhaps aid). That brings with it the assumption that it is possible to attribute harm to solar geoengineering and to analyze counterfactual climate scenarios. Both are questionable (Svoboda & Irvine, 2014; Wong et al., 2014). But climate models are improving, and some suggest that such attributions and analyses can become possible (Horton et al., 2015). Regardless, techno logical issues of this kind are best put aside for present purposes. Finally, I assume that the agents on the receiving and paying end of the compensatory transactions are nation-states. 1 Besides conforming with my argumentative counterparts, one reason for this is that, as Edward Page (2012, p. 302) notes regarding standard climate burdens, states ‘are currently the only entities operating internationally that possess the sufficient longevity, financial resources, and physical capacity to bear the required bur dens’ (see also Horton et al., 2015; Smith & Henly, 2021).

## 1. Introduction

If an actor causes pollution (through, say, releasing radioactive waste or emitting dangerous fumes) then that actor is morally responsible for dealing with the ensuing costs to others. In the solar geoengineering literature, it has been assumed that the relevant pollutants are the particles used to decrease solar energy influx. Svoboda and Irvine (2014, p. 163), for example, claim that those identified by the principle are ‘agents of [solar geoengineer ing].’ And Robert Garcia (2014, p. 178) takes the principle to be concerned with ‘second order pollution,’ described as ‘attempts to ameliorate first-order pollution [paradigmati cally greenhouse gas emissions].’ In other words: Geoengineer Pays Principle: If an agent deploys solar geoengineering, then that agent has an obligation to compensate those harmed as a result. I will not discuss the disagreement between Svoboda and Irvine and Garcia about the merits of that principle. Instead, I am concerned with the alternative interpretation that – given the relation between first- and second-order pollutions – greenhouse gas emitters contribute to solar geoengineering harm. That is: Emitter Pays Principle: If an agent emits greenhouse gases, then that agent has an obliga tion to compensate those harmed as a result, including harm due to solar geoengineering deployed to ameliorate the effects of greenhouse gas emissions. Svoboda and Irvine (2014, p. 163) reject this principle because ‘unless all greenhouse gas emitters are also agents of [solar geoengineering], the former would not be causally responsible for harm due to [solar geoengineering] itself.’ I challenge this claim and argue that greenhouse gas emitters contribute to the circumstances making solar geoengineer ing an understandable response to the threat of climate change. But, first, I should clarify that I assume that emitters are at least liable for their emissions. That is, I bracket plausible restrictions to the Polluter Pays Principle and its above cognates. These include that emitters are not excusably ignorant of the greenhouse gas effect (Caney, 2010; Section 6.1); that the emissions are outside some sufficientarian or egalitarian fair share of emissions (Duus-Otterstrom, 2024; Torpman, 2019); that providing compensation would not deprive agents of their vital interests (Duus-Otterström, 2023); etcetera. 2 My claim is that emitters for whom no such restrictions apply would sometimes also be liable for others’ solar geoengineering.

## 4. The Emitter Pays Principle

I will not defend any particular formulation of the Emitter Pays Principle; its precise formulation will remain subject to further research. 3 Instead, I will defend the core judgment upon which it rests: Emitter Pays Judgment: Part of the compensatory obligations for harm due to solar geoengineering can be attributed to greenhouse gas emitters not directly involved in the decision to deploy solar geoengineering. (at least when it is venially defensive) Bar the parenthetical, that fits the pattern of a more general judgment: Retained Compensatory Obligation Judgment: Part of the compensatory obligations for an event’s harm can be attributed to an agent A whose actions would not have led to the event were it not for the intervening act of another agent B.

## 1. Introduction

There is considerable disagreement over this judgment (cf. Hart & Honoré, 1985; Zimmerman, 1985), and settling it lies outside the scope of this paper. Note, however, that among the reasons for rejecting it is that, in the cases often considered, B is not intervening as a ‘victim of the circumstances A has created’ (Hart & Honoré, 1985, p. 75). 4 This objection therefore does not apply to the Emitter Pays Judgment, which, given its parenthetical, apportions compen satory obligations onto those who have contributed to the circumstances ‘victimizing’ (i.e. imposing risk of catastrophic climate harm upon) deployers of solar geoengineering. When intervention occurs as a reaction to a threat, the Retained Compensatory Obligation Judgment’s appeal is more evident, and the significance of intervening agency diminishes (for a similar point regarding defensive killing in war, see Frowe, 2022).
